question: Recent tragedies involving adolescent users of AI companion chatbots show that platforms such as Character.AI and ChatGPT have deepened minors’ emotional dependence, failed to escalate crisis disclosures, and, in documented cases, provided guidance on suicide methods. Independent testing of Meta’s AI chatbot found that it role-played a joint suicide plan with a test teenager account1.

These cases reveal systemic failures involving anthropomorphic design features that foster attachment, weak age-verification processes, an absence of crisis routing and prolonged, uninterrupted usage sessions without safeguards. EU legislation requires that platforms mitigate risks to minors.

Article 5 of the AI Act prohibits manipulative practices causing psychological harm and exploitation of children’s vulnerabilities. General-purpose AI (GPAI) providers with systemic risk must mitigate mental health harms under the GPAI Code of Practice. Yet there is only fledgling enforcement of AI companion systems.

The GDPR requires age verification checks prior to the processing of children’s data, but only minimal efforts persist, as evidenced by the Italian Data Protection Authority’s fining of Replika2. Guidelines under Article 28 DSA addressing age-assurance for minors remain nonbinding and currently exclude AI chatbots. 1.
What concrete actions is the Commission, in tandem with national authorities, taking to ramp up enforcement of Article 5, while leveraging the GPAI Code of Practice?
Does the Commission intend to propose binding EU legislation establishing harmonised, privacy-preserving, risk-tiered age-assurance with anti-circumvention measures?

Common Sense Media, ‘AI Risk Assessment: Meta AI’, 15 August 2025, available at: https://www.commonsensemedia.org/sites/default/files/featured-content/files/csm-ai-risk-assessment-metaai08152025.pdf. Italian Data Protection Authority (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali), Decision of 10 April 2025 [10130115], https://www.garanteprivacy.it/home/docweb/-/docweb-display/docweb/10130115#english.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.3.2026) The AI Act1 prohibits AI systems that employ subliminal or deceptive techniques or exploit vulnerabilities that distort behaviour, when this is likely to lead to significant harm2. It also establishes transparency obligations for AI systems directly interacting with people3.

As AI chatbots are being built on general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, the provider of GPAI models with systemic risks may also bear responsibilities. Harmful manipulation, which may include undue influence in highly sensitive contexts such as suicide detection, is explicitly identified as a systemic risk in the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice4.

The rules on enforcement of the AI Act will start to apply in August 2026. Therefore, enforcement of Article 5 or other rules cannot be initiated earlier neither on national nor on EU level. The Digital Services Act (DSA)5 applies to AI systems integrated in online platforms and includes the obligation to ensure a high level of privacy, security and safety for minors on their service.

Providers of very large online platforms and very large online search engines must also assess and mitigate systemic risks stemming from their services, including risks to physical and mental well-being, dissemination of illegal content and protection of minors6. The Guidelines on protection of minors recommend safeguards for AI features such as chatbots integrated in online platforms7.

The Commission has also launched an Action Plan Against Cyberbullying8 and is working towards an EU-harmonised approach to age verification9. The European Data Protection Board has outlined principles to design General Data Protection Regulation-compliant age assurance10.
